problem: Prior traversability-prediction and navigation systems fail to generalize across terrains, weather, lighting and embodiments, and naive sample-based planners with a fixed traversability/goal cost weight get stuck in local minima or oscillate between similarly scored paths.
motivation: Real-world outdoor navigation (e.g. Earth Rover Challenge) uses low-cost robots with noisy sensors, no onboard compute and high-latency 4G links, so SLAM-style pipelines are impractical. Systems must recognize traversable areas from a single RGB image under strong distribution shift, and plan robustly over long horizons. The 2024 ERC best autonomous system reached only 36% of the maximum score.
key_idea: Fine-tune SAM2 with a learnable traversability prompt token on a geographically diverse dataset, project the mask to a BEV cost map via a ground-plane assumption, and plan at path level by clustering and merging low-cost sampled paths, then choosing the one best aligned with the goal heading.
insight: Path-level fusion is far more reliable than pixel-level cost tuning: without fusion, path selection accuracy stays at 27–43% for every beta, while merging plus angular selection reaches 85.7%. Full encoder fine-tuning and diverse data matter for generalization: IoU rises from 0.8662 (single scene) to 0.9289 (full data) on Normal, and from 0.8215 (decoder-only D1) to 0.9262 on cross-embodiment.
method: SAM-TP: SAM2.1 Hiera-tiny with the prompt encoder removed and a learnable 'traversable' prompt token; the full image encoder and mask decoder are fine-tuned (Adam, lr 1e-6, batch 20, 10 epochs, <4h on one A100).
Semi-automatic annotation: SAM2 proposals are refined by humans in a lightweight GUI, giving 15,347 frames; masks cover only regions directly reachable from the robot.

BEV projection: no depth is used. Traversable pixels are assumed to lie on the ground plane, and the scale is solved from the known camera height (s·d_y = -h) using a generic camera model for calibration and lens distortion.
Path sampling and cost: random first/second-order polynomial paths are generated once; each planning cycle only re-evaluates their cost on the BEV map, then the top-K lowest-cost paths are kept.

Path fusion: adaptive k-means (k chosen by silhouette score) on waypoint-wise Euclidean distance, then centroids within a threshold are merged (precision preferred over recall); if several paths remain, the one with heading most aligned with the goal is chosen.

Closed-loop control: synchronous replan–align–advance 1 m loop, with a parallel collision-avoidance check on the traversability map that halts motion for near hazards (SAM-TP at 10 Hz on an RTX 3090, planner ~5 Hz).
VLM-assisted recovery: when stuck in a dead end, a VLM is asked from recent observations how to return to the previously navigable route.

setting.backbone: SAM2.1 Hiera-tiny (fine-tuned as SAM-TP) for traversability; heuristic path fusion planner; VLM for recovery
setting.model_size: SAM2.1 Hiera-tiny (~39M params, not stated in paper)
setting.training_data: 15,347 annotated road frames from FrodoBot dataset (collected in 7 countries; the intro says 20 countries), semi-automatically annotated with SAM2 masks plus human correction
setting.observation: monocular front RGB (3–5 Hz) plus GPS goal; IMU and wheel encoders available; known camera height
setting.action_space: waypoint following: align heading then advance 1 m (linear/angular velocity commands over 4G)
setting.privileged: none (known camera height prior and GPS checkpoints)

numbers.extra: remote inference on RTX 3090; 6 countries, 3 continents; max score 30

numbers.eval_set_note: human-annotated road images with varying branches

numbers_note: Path-fusion test set size is not stated. The intro says 20 countries for training data but the method section says seven; the benchmark is stated as 18 countries (intro) and 17 countries (method).
results: GeNIE placed first at ERC 2025 with 23.78/30 (79%) and zero interventions, versus 0.62 for the second-best team (Team A, 1 intervention). SAM-TP beats WVN, SAM, and Gemini-2.5-flash on all traversability splits (IoU 0.9289/0.7989/0.9262). Path fusion with angular selection reaches 85.7% path selection accuracy versus at most 42.9% without fusion.
limitations: Single-frame traversability with no local map or memory causes local minima (one zero-score mission where the robot refused the only viable low-traversability passage).
Conservative observe–plan–execute–wait control is inefficient under latency and caused timeouts in two missions.
Flat-ground BEV assumption and a single traversability token may fail on steep slopes or for different embodiments such as legged robots.
